lines.text: Ancient ruins, a hero who held off an empire, four centuries of Ottoman rule, then the most closed state in Europe. This is the story of Albania.
In the south, near the Greek border, Greeks and then Romans built the city of Butrint. Its ruins are now a World Heritage Site.
In the fifteenth century, the lord Skanderbeg led the Albanians against the Ottomans for a quarter of a century, and became the national hero.
Under Ottoman rule, in 1614, the town of Tirana was founded. Three centuries later it would become the capital.
Ali Pasha, an Albanian-born Ottoman governor, ruled much of the western Balkans almost as his own kingdom.
Ahmet Zog, born in 1895, would become president and then king, until Italy invaded in 1939.
Enver Hoxha, born in 1908, would rule as a communist for forty years and cut Albania off from the world.
Born to an Albanian family in 1910, Mother Teresa would found the Missionaries of Charity in Kolkata, and win the Nobel Peace Prize.
After more than four hundred years as part of the Ottoman Empire, Albania became an independent country in 1912.
On the twenty-eighth of November, at the port of Vlore, its leaders declared that Ottoman rule was over.
Ramiz Alia, born in 1925, would succeed Hoxha and let the closed state begin to open.
Ismail Kadare, born in 1936, would write The General of the Dead Army and become the best-known Albanian writer.
Edi Rama, born in 1964, a painter turned politician, would become prime minister in 2013.
From the late sixties, Hoxha had hundreds of thousands of concrete bunkers built across the land, against an invasion that never came.
Communism ended in 1991, but in 1997 pyramid schemes collapsed, wiping out savings and bringing the country to chaos.
Albania recovered, and in 2009 it joined NATO, and set its course toward the European Union.
From Skanderbeg's mountains to an open country, Albania's story moves on.
